passage:
In the Friday planning meeting, Uma proposed that all the team’s meetings go online. Six of the seven nodded. Jahnavi, the seventh, did not; she sat with her pen still.
“Can I say why I’m hesitant?” Jahnavi asked. “I think new joiners learn a lot by sitting in the room. But you’re right that the commute takes up hours, and that’s a real cost.”
Uma tilted her head. “So, what would work?”
“Try it for a month with one in-person day for new people, and see how they feel. If the numbers show I’m wrong, I’ll say so.”
Uma smiled. “That works. Let’s track it.”

qa.q: What did Uma propose in the Friday meeting?
qa.a: Uma proposed that all the team's meetings go online.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she asked to say why she was hesitant?
qa.a: Jahnavi was careful and calm, wanting to be heard without a fight. Acknowledging the commute cost shows she respects the other view.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi keep her integrity without needing to win?
qa.a: Jahnavi explained her reasoning, named what was valid in the majority's view and proposed a trial with a way to check the results. She agreed to say so if she was wrong.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt hearing Jahnavi's reply?
qa.a: Uma was probably relieved that the disagreement stayed friendly and became a plan. Tilting her head and asking what would work shows openness.

grounding: Shows a person who disagrees calmly, acknowledges what is valid in the other view, and is willing to be persuaded.

passage:
“Motion carried,” said Sudha, the society secretary, looking around the flat’s courtyard. “Who’s against the new gate?”
Himani raised her hand. “I am. But can I explain?”
“Go ahead,” said Sudha.
“I worry that a gate will make the old people feel locked out when the guard isn’t there. But I agree with what Mr. Rao said. Break-ins have gone up. That’s real.”
Mr. Rao nodded. “Thank you.”
“Could we try it for three months and add a bell for deliveries?” Himani asked. “If it works, I’ll happily be wrong.”
The others murmured. Sudha wrote it down.

qa.q: Who is the society secretary?
qa.a: Sudha is the society secretary.

qa.q: What is Himani worried about, and what does she accept?
qa.a: Himani worries that the gate will make older residents feel locked out when the guard is away. She accepts that break-ins have gone up, so she does not dismiss the other side's concern.

qa.q: How does Himani's request for a three-month trial keep the discussion respectful?
qa.a: She offers a test and a bell for deliveries and says she will happily be wrong. She does not need to win to say what she thinks.

qa.q: How might Mr. Rao have felt when Himani agreed with his point?
qa.a: Mr. Rao probably felt heard and thankful, since he nodded and thanked her. Being recognised made the disagreement less personal.

grounding: Shows a person disagreeing with the group calmly, acknowledging what is valid and open to being persuaded.

passage: Last month our team voted on replacing the phone helpline with a chatbot. I disagreed: many of our customers are elderly and struggle with typing. At the meeting I said so calmly, and I also said what I thought the others had right: the helpline was expensive, and the waits were long. Tenzin, who led the proposal, asked if I'd read the pilot results. I hadn't. I asked to see them before deciding. They showed younger customers loved the chatbot. I still thought elderly customers needed a phone option, and I said so, once, without heat. We voted eight to one. I lost. Afterwards Tenzin said, 'You made me add a call-back button for the over-sixties.' I'm Hafsa, and I didn't need to win to feel okay about that meeting.

qa.q: What did the team vote to replace the helpline with?
qa.a: A chatbot.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after losing the vote?
qa.a: Hafsa felt at peace, without needing to win, since the view had been stated honestly and calmly.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that kept the disagreement respectful?
qa.a: Acknowledged the valid points about cost and waits, asked to see the pilot results, and stated the view once, without heat.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Hafsa's objection?
qa.a: As useful rather than hostile, since it led Tenzin to add a call-back button for the over-sixties.

grounding: A person disagrees with the team calmly, grants what is valid in the other view, stays open to persuasion and keeps their integrity after losing.

passage: Supervisor's note, programme meeting, Thursday. The team discussed moving our village health camps from Sundays to Saturdays. Everyone agreed except Sonali. She explained that many women in two of our villages work in the fields on Saturdays and would miss the camp. She added that she understood the team's reason: our doctors are more available on Saturdays. Chinmay pushed back hard. Sonali didn't argue louder. She asked, 'Could we try Saturday in three villages and keep Sunday in the two where women work?' Chinmay said that would complicate the schedule. She said, 'Fair. I'll go with the group if we review attendance after a month.' We agreed. I noted how calm the room stayed throughout.

qa.q: Why did Sonali think some women would miss a Saturday camp?
qa.a: Many women in two of the villages work in the fields on Saturdays.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Sonali stayed calm and offered a compromise?
qa.a: Probably less defensive, since she acknowledged the team's reasons and didn't argue louder.

qa.q: What made Sonali's disagreement constructive?
qa.a: She explained her reasoning, acknowledged the doctors' availability, offered a trial, and agreed to go with the group if attendance was reviewed.

qa.q: How did the supervisor experience the meeting?
qa.a: The supervisor noticed and valued how calm the room stayed throughout the disagreement.

grounding: A team member disagrees calmly, acknowledges the other side's reasons and is willing to be persuaded, keeping the room calm.

passage:
Diary, Sunday.
Book club today. Everyone except me wanted to drop next month's novel because the author said something silly online. Uday said reading it would 'support' the author. I said I disagreed, and why: the book is about migrant workers, and I think the story matters more than the author's post. I also said Uday had a point, that it's fair not to want to buy it. Then I asked, 'What if we borrow library copies?' Nobody agreed. Uday said I was being stubborn. I said, 'Maybe. Convince me.' He did change my mind about buying new copies. He didn't change my mind about the book.
We're skipping it. I'll read it on my own and still come next month. That's fine.
Rajni

qa.q: What is next month's novel about?
qa.a: Migrant workers.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel about the outcome?
qa.a: Rajni feels calm and settled, fine with losing the vote while keeping personal convictions.

qa.q: What made Rajni's disagreement respectful?
qa.a: Explaining the reasoning, granting Uday's valid point, suggesting library copies and saying 'Convince me', open to being persuaded.

qa.q: How might Uday see Rajni's 'Maybe. Convince me'?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, finding it hard to call Rajni stubborn when Rajni openly invites persuasion.

grounding: A person disagrees with the group calmly, grants a valid point, is partly persuaded and keeps their integrity without needing to win.
